say.straight: Step (next key), third (skip one), fifth (count to five), octave (count to eight). Count keys in the scale from one.
say.eli5: A step is the very next key. A third skips one. A fifth is five keys along. An octave is eight along, and sounds like the same note but higher.

say.mentor: Build a phrase on a jump. Press rec, then play the first key, jump to the third or the fifth, and come back down by steps. Try it a couple of times with different jumps and keep the one you like.
say.straight: Record a phrase: first key, jump to the third or fifth, step back down. At least three different notes.
say.eli5: Press rec. Play the first key. Jump up to the third or the fifth. Then walk back down one key at a time.

steps.q: What is an interval?
steps.why: The distance between two notes, counted in steps.

whyWrong.1: That's a different kind of gap.
whyWrong.2: Scales are made of intervals, but they're not the same thing.
whyWrong.3: Loudness is amplitude.

steps.q: Counting from one, which key is the fifth?
steps.why: Count the start as one; the fifth is five keys along.

whyWrong.1: The second key is a step.
whyWrong.2: The eighth key is the octave.
whyWrong.3: Twelve half steps is an octave.

steps.q: How do small intervals usually feel in a melody?
steps.why: Steps feel smooth. Big jumps feel dramatic.

whyWrong.1: That's big intervals.
whyWrong.2: Both are sounds.
whyWrong.3: Interval is pitch, not speed.

steps.next: Next: writing a melody. A motif, repeat it, change one note.

lessons.title: writing a melody

song.why: a good melody repeats enough to remember and changes enough to stay interesting

lessons.learn: The simplest way to write a melody that sticks: a short motif, played again, with one note changed.
youCan: say what a motif is
write a melody by repeating and changing a motif
hear question and answer phrases

say.mentor: Low, then high. Two notes is already the start of a tune. The trick most hooks use is simple: a short idea, called a motif, then the same idea again with one small change. Your ear loves hearing something come back, and loves a little surprise when it does.
say.straight: Most hooks are a short motif, repeated, with one change. Repetition makes it stick; the change keeps it interesting.
say.eli5: Here's the secret of catchy tunes: play a little tune, then play it again but change one note. Your brain loves hearing it come back, with a tiny surprise.

say.mentor: Think of a melody as a conversation. The first half asks a question: it ends somewhere that feels unfinished, maybe up high. The second half answers: same shape, but it lands back home on the first key of your scale. Say it out loud: da da da daa? da da da dum.
say.straight: Phrase one ends unfinished (a question), phrase two repeats it and lands on the home note (an answer).
say.eli5: A tune can ask a question and then answer it. The first part ends up in the air. The second part is nearly the same, but it comes home to the first key.

say.mentor: Write it. Press rec and play a motif of three or four notes in the first half of the bar. In the second half, play it again, but change the last note so it lands on the first key. Record it as many times as you like until it sounds like a tune you'd hum.
say.straight: Record a motif in the first half of the bar, then repeat it in the second half ending on the first key.
say.eli5: Press rec. Play three or four notes. Then play the same notes again, but make the last one the very first key. That's your melody!

steps.q: What is a motif?
options: a short musical idea that repeats
steps.why: A short idea, often three or four notes, that a melody is built from.

whyWrong.1: A motif is much smaller than a song.
whyWrong.2: Drums can have motifs too, but here it's a few notes of melody.
whyWrong.3: A scale is the set of notes; a motif is what you play with them.

steps.q: What makes an answer phrase feel finished?
options: it lands on the home note, the first key
steps.why: Landing on the first note of the scale feels like coming home.

whyWrong.1: Volume doesn't finish a phrase.
whyWrong.2: Speed doesn't either.
whyWrong.3: It's where it lands, not how many notes.

steps.q: Why repeat the motif with one change instead of something totally new?
options: repetition sticks, the change keeps it interesting
steps.why: Your ear remembers what comes back and enjoys the small surprise.

whyWrong.1: It's about how it sounds, not effort.
whyWrong.2: You can play anything you like.
whyWrong.3: Length isn't the reason.

steps.next: Next: the pentatonic hook. Five notes, no wrong ones.

lessons.title: the pentatonic hook

song.why: five notes with no clashes make it easy to play a hook that always fits

lessons.learn: The five-note scale behind countless hooks and solos, and a hook of your own played on it.
youCan: say what a pentatonic scale is
find the five notes on your keys
play a hook using only those five

say.mentor: Some of the catchiest melodies ever use only five notes. Take a minor scale, drop the two notes most likely to clash, and you get the minor pentatonic. It's in blues, rock solos, African and Asian folk music, and a lot of dance hooks, because nothing in it can sound wrong over the chords.
say.straight: The minor pentatonic: a minor scale minus the two notes most likely to clash. Five notes, no wrong ones, used everywhere.
say.eli5: Take your seven notes and leave out two. The five that are left all get along perfectly. That's called a pentatonic scale.

say.mentor: On your keys, the minor pentatonic is keys one, three, four, five and seven, counting from the first. Skip two and six. In a minor that's a, c, d, e and g. Try it: run up those five and down again, and hear how open and singable it is.
say.straight: Keys 1, 3, 4, 5, 7 of your minor scale. Skip 2 and 6.
say.eli5: Use keys one, three, four, five and seven. Skip key two and key six.

say.mentor: Make a hook on those five. Press rec and play a short phrase using only keys one, three, four, five and seven. Keep it simple: hooks are short, rhythmic and repeat. Record it until you'd want to hear it again.
say.straight: Record a short hook using only keys 1, 3, 4, 5 and 7.
say.eli5: Press rec and play a little tune using only keys one, three, four, five and seven.

steps.hint: Short and repeated beats long and complicated.

steps.q: How many notes are in a pentatonic scale?
steps.why: Penta means five.

whyWrong.1: Seven is a full major or minor scale.
whyWrong.2: Twelve is every note.
whyWrong.3: Three notes is a chord.

steps.q: Why is the pentatonic so easy to play hooks on?
options: the notes that clash most are left out
steps.why: Dropping the two clashiest notes leaves five that always fit.

whyWrong.1: It's about which notes, not volume.
whyWrong.2: It covers every octave.
whyWrong.3: Scales don't set the tempo.

steps.q: Which keys of your minor scale make the minor pentatonic?
steps.why: Leave out two and six.

whyWrong.1: Close, but it skips two and includes seven.
whyWrong.2: Those are some of the ones you leave out.
whyWrong.3: That's the full scale.

steps.next: Next: chords. Three notes at once, and the harmony under your melody.

lessons.title: what are chords?

song.why: chords are the harmony under your melody, the colour of the whole song

lessons.learn: What a chord is, how three notes make one, major and minor chords by ear, and chords in your song.
youCan: say what a chord and a triad are
hear a major chord from a minor one
play chords into your song

say.mentor:
One note on its own is a line. Play three notes from your scale at once, skipping a key between each, and you get a chord: a little cloud of harmony that colours everything played over it.
That stack of three, the first, third and fifth, is called a triad. It's the building block of almost every song.
say.straight: A chord is several notes at once. The basic one is a triad: a note, the third above it and the fifth.
say.eli5: Play three notes at the same time and you get a chord. It's like three friends singing together. The main kind uses notes one, three and five.

say.mentor:
Like scales, chords come in major and minor, and you can hear it straight away: major chords sound bright, minor ones darker. The only difference is the middle note, the third, moved by one key.
The chord pads in the next step are labelled the way musicians write them: big letters for major, small for minor. Roman numerals say which note of the scale the chord starts on.
say.straight: Major chords sound bright, minor darker. The difference is the third, one key apart. Pads use roman numerals: capitals major, lower case minor.
say.eli5: Some chords sound happy (major), some sound a bit sad (minor). The pads have little names on them: big letters for happy chords, small letters for sad ones.

deeper.title: why skip a key
deeper.say: Notes right next to each other rub and buzz. Skipping one each time gives notes that share harmonics, so they blend. That's the harmonic series from the harmonics lesson again.

say.mentor: Put chords in your song. Press rec, wait out the count-in, and play two chords: one at the start of the bar, one halfway. Start on i, the home chord, and try any other for the second. Hold each one down for a while so it rings.
say.straight: Record two chords into your song: i at the start of the bar, any other halfway.
say.eli5: Press rec, wait for four ticks. Press the first chord pad and hold it. Halfway through, press a different one.

steps.q: What is a triad?
options: three notes: a root, its third and its fifth
steps.why: Root, third and fifth, the basic chord.

whyWrong.1: That's time, not harmony.
whyWrong.2: That's a playlist.
whyWrong.3: Drums have no pitch to make chords.

steps.q: What makes a chord major or minor?
steps.why: Move the third by one key and the chord flips between major and minor.

whyWrong.1: Volume doesn't change the chord.
whyWrong.2: Length doesn't either.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is the song's speed.

steps.q: On the chord pads, what does a capital roman numeral mean?
steps.why: Capitals for major, lower case for minor.

whyWrong.1: Minor is lower case.
whyWrong.2: It's about the chord's colour.
whyWrong.3: Numerals say which note it starts on.

steps.next: Next: chord progressions. Four chords in a row and how they pull you along.

lessons.title: chord progressions

song.why: chords that move in a good order carry the listener through the song

lessons.learn: How chords move from one to the next, the progressions behind countless songs, and four chords in your song.
youCan: say what a chord progression is
play a four chord progression
hear which chord feels like home

say.mentor: A chord progression is just chords in an order. Some orders feel like a journey: away from home and back again. Four chords, round and round, is the backbone of a huge amount of pop and dance music.
say.straight: A progression is a sequence of chords. Four chords looping is the backbone of most pop and dance tracks.
say.eli5: Chords in a row make a progression, like a little journey. Most songs use four chords going round and round.

say.mentor:
Your i chord is home. Every other chord pulls a little away from it, and the progression feels satisfying when it comes back. In minor, a classic is i, VI, III, VII: home, then three steps that each feel like they're heading somewhere, then home again on the loop.
You've heard it in countless tracks. Once you know it, you'll hear it everywhere.
say.straight: i is home. Others pull away. In minor, i VI III VII is a classic four chord loop.
say.eli5: The first chord is home. The others go on an adventure. Then the loop brings you home again. Try i, VI, III, VII.

deeper.title: four chords everywhere
deeper.say: The same four chords, in major or minor order, sit under an enormous number of hits. Producers don't worry about that: the sound, rhythm and melody on top are what make a track yours.

say.mentor: Play a four chord progression into your song, one chord on each beat. Start on i, then try VI, III and VII, or any order you like. Listen for which one makes you want to go back to i.
say.straight: Record four chords, one per beat, starting on i. Try i VI III VII or your own order.
say.eli5: Press rec. Play four chord pads, one on each tick. Start with i, then try VI, III and VII.

steps.q: What is a chord progression?
steps.why: A sequence of chords, often looped.

whyWrong.1: A scale is single notes.
whyWrong.2: One chord isn't a progression.
whyWrong.3: Fills are drums.

steps.q: In your scale, which chord feels like home?
steps.why: The chord built on the first note of the scale is home.

whyWrong.1: VII pulls back toward i.
whyWrong.2: Loudness doesn't decide home.
whyWrong.3: It's about the note it's built on.

steps.q: How many chords are in a lot of pop and dance loops?
steps.why: Four chords, round and round, is the most common loop.

whyWrong.1: One chord can work, but it's not a progression.
whyWrong.2: Twelve would be very busy.
whyWrong.3: That's a lot for a loop.

steps.next: Next: bass follows the chords. Root notes under your progression.

lessons.title: bass follows the chords

song.why: a bass on the root of each chord glues the harmony to the beat

lessons.learn: What a root note is, why the bass usually plays it, and a bass line under your chords.
youCan: say what a root note is
play a bass line that follows your chords
hear how the bass holds the harmony together

say.mentor:
Listen to the low one. Low notes carry a lot of weight: they tell your ear which chord it's hearing. That's why the simplest bass line is just the bottom note of each chord, played low.
That bottom note is called the root, the note the chord is named after.
say.straight: Low notes define the chord. The simplest bass line plays the root, the note each chord is built on.
say.eli5: Low notes are like the floor a chord stands on. The easiest bass line just plays the lowest note of each chord. That note is called the root.

say.mentor: Play the root of each of your chords on the bass. The bass keys are low versions of your scale, so key one is the root of i, key six the root of VI, key three of III, key seven of VII. Press rec and play the roots in the same order as your chords, one per chord.
say.straight: Record the roots of your chords on the bass keys, in order. Key number matches the numeral: i is one, VI is six, III three, VII seven.
say.eli5: Press rec. Play the bass key with the same number as each chord: one for i, six for VI, three for III, seven for VII.

say.mentor: Hear how the song suddenly sits down? The bass locks the chords to the kick. Producers spend ages on this relationship, because the bass and the kick both live down low and can fight. In the producer world you'll learn to make room for both.
say.straight: The bass ties the chords to the beat. Bass and kick share the low end, so they need room; you'll fix that in the producer world.
say.eli5: Now your song has a floor under it! The bass and the boom both live down low, so later you'll learn how to make them share.

steps.q: What is a root note?
options: the note a chord is named after and built on
steps.why: The root is the bottom note the chord is built up from.

whyWrong.1: Usually it's the lowest, not highest, in a basic chord.
whyWrong.2: Drums have no root.
whyWrong.3: It's a note, not a song.

steps.q: Why does the bass often play the root?
options: low notes tell the ear which chord it is
the root is the loudest note
the bass can't play other notes
steps.why: Low notes carry the most weight, so the root defines the chord.

whyWrong.1: It's about sound, not effort.
whyWrong.2: Volume is up to you.
whyWrong.3: A bass can play anything.

steps.q: Your chord is VI. Which bass key plays its root?
steps.why: The numeral tells you the scale note it starts on.

whyWrong.1: Key one is the root of i.
whyWrong.2: Key three is III.
whyWrong.3: Key seven is VII.

steps.next: Next: tension, release and structure. Your loop becomes a song with an intro and a drop.

lessons.title: samples and loops

song.why: recorded sounds bring a real room and real hits into your song

lessons.learn: What a sample is, how loops are built from them, and real recorded drums playing your own beat.
youCan: say what a sample and a loop are
hear the difference between a synth and a recorded drum
put recorded drums in your song

say.mentor: A sample is a recording you play back as an instrument: a single drum hit, a vocal, a chord from an old record. A loop is a sample that repeats, usually a bar or two long. Hip hop was built on loops cut from funk and soul records, and house producers sample constantly.
say.straight: A sample is a recording used as an instrument. A loop is a sample that repeats.
say.eli5: A sample is a recorded sound you can play like an instrument. A loop is a sample that goes round and round.

deeper.title: sampling and permission
deeper.say: Using a few seconds of someone else's record still needs permission if you release it. Lots of producers record their own sounds or use sample packs that come cleared. The drums here were recorded for CCD School and are free to use.

say.mentor: Here's your beat. The drums so far have been made by the engine. Switch to recorded and the same pattern plays on real recorded hits: a kick, a clap, a hat and a snare. Listen to the texture.
say.straight: Your beat on synth drums or recorded samples. Pick one.
say.eli5: Same beat, made by the computer or played on real recorded drums. Which sounds better to you?

steps.q: What is a sample?
options: a recording used as an instrument
steps.why: Any recording you play back as an instrument.

whyWrong.1: A melody can be sampled, but a sample is any recording.
whyWrong.2: Waves are synthesis.
whyWrong.3: A drum machine may play samples, but it isn't one.

steps.q: What is a loop?
steps.why: A bar or two of audio that plays round and round.

whyWrong.1: A single hit is a one-shot.
whyWrong.2: A chorus is a section.
whyWrong.3: Reverb is space.

steps.next: Next: tension, release and structure. Your loop becomes a song.

lessons.title: tension, release and structure

song.why: a song is a loop that changes over time

lessons.learn: How songs build and release tension, the sections of a dance track, and your loop arranged into a song.
youCan: say what tension and release mean in music
name an intro, build, drop and break
arrange your loop into sections

say.mentor: Music works by building tension and releasing it. A chord that wants to go home, a drum roll before a change, the drums dropping out so their return feels huge. Dance music does this with arrangement: the same loop, with parts taken away and brought back.
say.straight: Tension builds, release pays it off. Dance tracks do it by taking parts away and bringing them back.
say.eli5: Songs make you wait for something, then give it to you. That waiting feeling is tension. Getting it is release.

say.mentor: Here's your loop laid out as a song: intro, build, drop, break, drop. Each row is one of your parts. Tap a square to switch a part off or on in that section, and tap fill for a drum roll at the end. Play it through. You've just made a song.
say.straight: Your loop as sections. Tap squares to switch parts off or on; tap fill for a roll.
say.eli5: Tap squares to turn sounds on and off in each part. Press play and hear your whole song.

steps.q: What is a breakdown?
options: a section with the drums taken out
steps.why: Drums out, so their return is a big release.

whyWrong.1: That's the drop.
whyWrong.2: It's on purpose.
whyWrong.3: That's the start of the intro.

steps.q: In music, what is release?
steps.why: Tension builds, release resolves it.

whyWrong.1: Loudness is separate.
whyWrong.2: Different meaning of the word.
whyWrong.3: That's a synth's release knob, a different idea.

steps.next: Next: the producer world. Make every part of your song sound its best.

lessons.title: bonus, higher or lower

song.why: nothing changes in your song here; this round trains the ears you use on every part of it

lessons.learn: A quick ear round: two notes, which one is higher? It gets harder as you get them right.
youCan: hear which of two notes is higher, even when they're close

say.mentor: A quick one, just for your ears. Tap low, then high. Easy when they're far apart. In the round coming up they start far apart and get closer together as you get them right, until it's a real test. Producers do this all day: is the bass a little too high, is that note a touch flat.
say.straight: Ear round: which of two notes is higher. They get closer as you get them right.
say.eli5: A listening game! You'll hear two notes. Say which one is higher. They start far apart and get closer and closer.

steps.say: Two notes. Which one was higher? Replay as often as you like.

steps.q: Two notes, one at 220 hz and one at 233 hz. Which is higher?
options: you can't tell from the numbers
steps.why: More wiggles a second, higher note. 233 is higher, though only a little.

whyWrong.1: 220 is the lower of the two.
whyWrong.2: They're 13 hz apart, about one key on a piano.
whyWrong.3: The bigger number is always the higher pitch.

steps.next: Back to your song: waveforms, and picking the shape for your melody.

lessons.title: bonus, your ear

song.why: nothing changes in your song here; this round trains the ears you use on every part of it

lessons.learn: A quick ear round on intervals and pitch: hear the jump, name the direction.
youCan: hear small and large pitch changes

say.mentor: An ear round. You know the octave by now. The round coming up asks which of two notes is higher, and the gap shrinks as you get them right. It's the same skill you use to hear a bass that's out of key or a lead that's a touch flat.
say.straight: Ear round: which of two notes is higher. The gap shrinks as you go.
say.eli5: A listening game. Two notes, which is higher? It gets trickier as you go.

steps.say: Which one was higher? Replay as often as you like.

steps.next: Back to your song: chords, and the harmony under your melody.

lessons.title: bonus, listen like a producer

song.why: nothing changes in your song here; you're learning to hear it like a producer

lessons.learn: How producers listen: one part at a time, then the whole, then the journey.
youCan: listen to one part of a track at a time
describe a track's structure by ear

say.mentor:
Producers listen in layers. First pick one part and follow only it for the whole track: just the hats, say. Then listen to the whole, and ask what's loudest, what's in front, what's far away. Then listen to the journey: when do things come in and go out, where's the drop, how long is the break.
Try it on your own song in the studio, then on a track you love.
say.straight: Listen to one part, then the balance, then the structure. Your song first, then a track you love.
say.eli5: Pick one sound and only listen to that. Then listen to everything. Then listen for when things change.

steps.q: What's a good first way to listen like a producer?
options: follow one part through the whole track
turn it up as loud as possible
steps.why: Following one part teaches you what each part is doing.

whyWrong.1: You'd miss the build that makes it work.
whyWrong.2: Loud hides detail.
whyWrong.3: The intro tells you a lot.

steps.next: The producer world is next: make every part of your song sound its best.

lessons.title: your kick

song.why: the kick is the heartbeat of a dance track, everything else is placed around it

lessons.learn: Your song starts here. By the end of this lesson it will have a kick drum on every beat, played in by you and shaped the way you like it.
youCan: count beats and bars at 120 bpm
play a kick in on the beat
tell a short kick from a long one
shape a kick with decay and tune

say.mentor:
That thump is a kick drum. It is the lowest, loudest drum in a dance track, and the one you feel in your chest. It works like the song's heartbeat: everything you add later lines up with it.
Just listen for a few seconds. Notice it never speeds up or slows down.
say.straight: This is a kick drum on its own. In dance music it carries the beat: it is the deepest, heaviest hit, and every other part is timed against it. Listen to how even it is. Same gap, every time.
say.eli5: Hear that boom, boom, boom? That is a kick drum, a big low drum. It is like a heartbeat for the song. It goes at the same speed the whole time, and all the other sounds will dance along with it.

say.mentor:
The kick is playing again. Count out loud with it: one, two, three, four, one, two, three, four. Each count is a beat. A group of four beats is a bar.
This song runs at 120 beats per minute, or bpm. That is two beats every second, so one bar takes exactly two seconds. Counting is how producers find their way around a song, so it is worth getting comfortable with now.
say.straight:
Every kick you hear is one beat. Beats come in groups of four, and each group is called a bar. Try counting one to four along with it and starting again at one.
The speed of a song is measured in beats per minute, bpm. Yours is 120, so you get two beats a second and a bar every two seconds. When a producer says "bring the bass in at bar 9", this is the counting they mean.
say.eli5:
Say it out loud with the boom: one, two, three, four. Then start again: one, two, three, four. Each boom is called a beat. Four beats together are called a bar, a bit like four steps make one little walk.
Your song plays 120 beats every minute. That means two booms every second, so one bar lasts two seconds.

deeper.title: why 120
deeper.say: House music usually sits between 120 and 128 bpm, so you are starting where a lot of dance floors live. Slower feels heavier and lazier. Faster feels more urgent.

deeper.title: why groups of four
deeper.say: Four beats to a bar is the most common count in dance music, because it is easy to feel and easy to move to. You will see it written as 4/4. Other counts exist, like the 3/4 of a waltz, and you will meet them later.

say.mentor:
Every song starts somewhere, and yours starts with a kick. You're going to record it now, and that bar becomes the loop everything else in your song sits on.
The click you hear is a metronome: a steady tick on every beat so you have something to play along to. Press rec. You get four clicks to count you in, so just listen. Then tap the kick pad once on each of the next four clicks. Try to land right on the click. Any kick that comes in early or late shows up red, so you can see it and play it again.
Missed one? Tap undo to take back the last hit, or hold it to start over.
say.straight:
A song needs a beat first, so you record the kick now. This one bar loops under everything you add.
The ticking is a metronome, there to keep you in time. Press rec and wait out the first four ticks, that is the count-in. On the next four ticks, tap the kick pad once each. Hits that miss the beat show red.
Undo removes your last tap. Hold undo to clear the bar and go again.
say.eli5:
To make a song, you need a kick first. So now you play yours, and it goes into your song.
Hear the tick, tick, tick? That is there to help you keep time, like someone clapping along. Press the red rec button. Let four ticks go by without tapping. Then tap the kick pad once on every tick, four times. If a tap is too early or too late, it turns red so you know to try that one again.
Made a mistake? Press undo to take back your last tap.

say.mentor:
What you just played has a name: four on the floor. A kick on every beat, never missing one.
It is the pulse under disco, house and most techno. It works because it is completely steady. Dancers lock onto it without thinking, and every part you add next, the hats, the bass, the chords, gets placed around those four hits.
say.straight:
A kick on all four beats of the bar is called four on the floor.
It is the standard house and techno beat. Its strength is that it never changes, which makes it easy to dance to and gives every other part of the song something solid to line up against.
say.eli5:
Booming on every single beat has a fun name: four on the floor. Four booms, all on the floor.
Lots of dance music does this, because a steady boom is really easy to dance to. Everything else you add later will fit around these four booms.

deeper.title: where it comes from
deeper.say: Disco drummers in the 1970s played the kick on every beat to keep dance floors moving. When Chicago producers made the first house records in the 1980s with drum machines, they kept that same kick, and it has been the backbone of dance music ever since.

deeper.title: songs to listen for it in
deeper.say: Donna Summer's I Feel Love, Daft Punk's Around the World, and almost any house or techno track you have heard in a club. Put one on and count along: the kick lands on every number.

deeper.title: other kinds of beat
deeper.say: Not every beat puts the kick everywhere. A breakbeat moves the kicks around, so they fall between beats too. Hip hop often has fewer kicks and leaves gaps. Two step and garage skip some beats on purpose. You will try these later. For now, four on the floor is the solid ground.

say.mentor:
Kicks come in different lengths. Tap short, then long, and listen to the end of each hit.
The short kick stops fast and leaves a gap before the next one. The long kick keeps humming through that gap, so the whole beat feels bigger and heavier. Neither is wrong. Short kicks feel punchy and tight, long kicks feel deep and boomy. Next you get to set your own.
say.straight:
Same kick, two lengths. Switch between short and long and pay attention to what happens after each hit.
Short kicks leave space between beats, which sounds tight and punchy. Long kicks fill that space, which sounds big and heavy. Both are used all the time, it depends on the track.
say.eli5:
Tap short, then tap long. Can you hear the difference?
The short one is like knocking on a table: knock, then quiet. The long one is like hitting a big empty barrel: it hums for a while after. Both are good. You will pick yours next.

say.mentor:
Every kick is made of two parts, and you can see both in the picture. First a click: a tiny, sharp tap right at the start that helps the kick cut through. Then the body: a low hum that starts high, drops quickly, and fades away.
Decay sets how long the body lasts. Turn it down for a short, punchy kick. Turn it up for a long, boomy one. Tune sets how low the body sits. Down makes it deeper, up makes it higher and tighter.
Your loop is playing, so turn and listen, and watch the picture change. Try decay first. Stop when it sounds like the kick you want.
say.straight:
The picture shows your kick as a wave. The sharp spike at the start is the click. The swinging part after it is the body, and the dotted line shows it fading out.
Decay controls how long the body takes to fade. Tune controls its pitch, how low or high it sits. Turn each one while the loop plays until the kick sounds right to you.
say.eli5:
The pink line is a drawing of your kick. See the quick little spike at the start? That is the click, like the tap of a finger. The wobbly part after it is the body, the big low hum.
The decay knob makes the hum shorter or longer. The tune knob makes it deeper or higher, like a big drum or a small drum. Your kick is playing, so turn them and listen. Stop when you like it.

steps.q: How many beats are in one bar here?
steps.why: You counted one, two, three, four, then started again. Each group of four is a bar.

whyWrong.1: Count along with the kick. It goes up to four before it starts over.
whyWrong.2: Eight beats is two bars. Count along again and listen for where it starts over at one.
whyWrong.3: Sixteen is the number of small steps in a bar, which you will meet in the hats lesson. A bar has four beats.

steps.q: What is a kick on every beat called?
steps.why: Four on the floor. A kick on every one of the four beats, the steady pulse under house and disco.

whyWrong.1: A breakbeat moves the kicks around so they fall between beats too. Yours lands on every beat.
whyWrong.2: A fill is a short burst that leads into a new section. Your kick just keeps going.
whyWrong.3: A bar is the group of four beats. The pattern of a kick on each of them has its own name.

steps.q: At 120 bpm, how long does one bar last?
steps.why: 120 beats a minute is two beats every second. Four beats in a bar takes two seconds.

whyWrong.1: One second only fits two beats at 120 bpm. A bar has four.
whyWrong.2: That would be 60 bpm, half the speed of your song.
whyWrong.3: Half a second is one beat. A bar is four of them.

steps.q: You want a short, punchy kick. What do you change?
steps.why: Decay sets how long the body lasts. Less decay, shorter kick, more punch.

whyWrong.1: More decay makes the body ring longer, which is the boomy kick.
whyWrong.2: Tune changes how high or low the kick sits, not how long it lasts.
whyWrong.3: Tune down makes it deeper, but it still rings just as long. Length is decay.

steps.q: What is the short, sharp sound at the very start of a kick?
steps.why: The click is the tiny tap at the start. The body is the low hum that comes right after it.

whyWrong.1: The body is the low hum after the start. The very first sharp bit is the click.
whyWrong.2: Decay is a knob. It sets how long the body lasts.
whyWrong.3: The metronome is the tick you played along to. It is not part of the kick.

steps.q: Your kick sounds thin and too high. What do you turn?
steps.why: Tune sets how low the body sits. Turning it down makes the kick deeper and fuller.

whyWrong.1: Decay changes the length. The kick would still sound thin, just shorter.
whyWrong.2: Tune up makes it even higher.
whyWrong.3: The click button turns the metronome on and off. It does not change your kick.

steps.q: Why does the metronome click while you record?
options: so you can play along in time
it is part of the song
to count how many kicks you played
steps.why: The click is a steady guide so your taps land on the beat. It is not recorded into your song.

whyWrong.1: The click is a separate sound and does not touch your kick.
whyWrong.2: The click is only a guide while you play. Your song does not include it.
whyWrong.3: It just ticks on every beat, so you have something to play along to.

steps.next: Next: what sound actually is, and how a synth makes it from nothing. That is where your first melody comes from.

lessons.title: sound, and your first synth

song.why: a synth line on top of your kick turns a beat into music

lessons.learn: What sound actually is, how a synth makes it out of nothing but numbers, and your first synth line playing over your kick.
youCan: explain what sound is, air pushed and pulled
hear how pitch is the speed of that push and pull
tell a soft wave, a saw and a square apart
play and shape your first synth line

say.mentor:
That is a synth playing one note. Before we touch the synth, here is what is actually happening when you hear it.
Look at the picture. The speaker cone moves out and in, very fast. Moving out, it shoves the air in front of it together. Moving in, it leaves the air spread thin. Those bunched and thin patches roll through the room to your ear, and your ear turns them into sound. That is all sound is: air being pushed and pulled.
say.straight:
One synth note. Every sound you hear works the same way: something moves back and forth and pushes the air around it.
In the picture the speaker cone moves out and in. Out squeezes the air together, in lets it spread. Those squeezed and spread patches travel to your ear, which reads them as sound.
say.eli5:
Hear that hum? It is a synth playing one note.
Watch the speaker on the left. It wiggles out and in really, really fast. Each wiggle pushes the air, like ripples when you drop a stone in water. The ripples travel across the room into your ear, and that is what you hear. Sound is just wiggling air.

say.mentor:
Tap low, then high. Same sound, different pitch.
One full push and pull of the air is called a cycle. Pitch is how many cycles happen every second. The low note pushes the air slowly, about 110 times a second. The high note does it four times as fast, about 440 times a second. Look at the wave: more cycles squeezed in means a higher note. We count cycles per second in hertz, written Hz.
say.straight:
Low, then high. Same tone, different pitch.
Pitch is the number of push and pull cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz). The low note here is about 110 Hz and the high one about 440 Hz. In the picture, more cycles across the same space means faster vibration and a higher note.
say.eli5:
Tap low, then tap high.
A low note wiggles the air slowly. A high note wiggles it fast. Look at the picture: the high one has lots of wiggles packed close together. One wiggle, out and back, is called a cycle. More cycles every second means a higher note.

deeper.title: how fast is fast
deeper.say: People hear from about 20 cycles a second, a rumble you feel more than hear, up to about 20,000, a whisper of a hiss. Your kick lives around 50. The A a band tunes to is 440.

say.mentor:
Now the really cool part. A guitar makes sound with a string, a voice with vocal cords. A synth has neither. It just calculates the shape of the wave, as a long run of numbers, and sends those numbers to the speaker. The speaker moves exactly that shape, and the air carries it to you. Any shape you can draw, a synth can play.
Tap soft, saw and square. Same note, three shapes. The round, soft wave sounds pure and gentle. The saw, a slope then a sudden drop, sounds bright and buzzy. The square, flat on top then flat on the bottom, sounds hollow, a bit like an old video game.
say.straight:
A synth has no string or reed. It computes the wave shape as numbers and the speaker turns those numbers into movement, which turns into moving air. So the shape is entirely up to you.
Switch between soft, saw and square. Same pitch, different shapes, different sound: smooth and pure, bright and buzzy, hollow and retro.
say.eli5:
Here is the magic bit. A guitar needs a string. Your voice needs your throat. A synth needs nothing like that. It just draws the wiggle using numbers, and the speaker copies the drawing by moving. So a synth can make any wiggle it wants.
Tap soft, saw and square. The soft one is smooth like a hum. The saw is buzzy like a bee. The square sounds like an old video game.

deeper.title: why the shape changes the sound
deeper.say: A smooth wave is just the one pitch. Sharp corners and sudden jumps add lots of extra, higher pitches on top, quietly. Your ear hears that mix as brightness or buzz. That is why the saw and square sound richer than the soft wave.

say.mentor:
Time to play your synth. Your kick is playing underneath, and anything you record goes on top of it as the first tune in your song.
Press rec, let the four clicks go by, then play any four or more keys. Every key here fits with the others, so nothing you press can sound wrong. Try a slow pattern first: one key per beat is plenty.
say.straight: Record your first synth line over the kick. Press rec, wait out the count-in, then play at least four notes. The keys are all from one scale, so any of them work together. Slow and simple is a good start.
say.eli5:
Your turn to play the synth! Your kick keeps going underneath.
Press rec, wait for four clicks, then press some keys. Any keys. They all sound nice together, so you cannot get it wrong. Go slow, one key at a time.

say.mentor: Now shape your synth while your line plays. Wave slides from saw to square, the same shapes you just heard. Cutoff is brightness: turn it down and the corners of the wave get rounded off, so the sound goes soft and dark. Turn it up for bright and buzzy. Watch the picture change as you turn.
say.straight: Shape your line while it loops. Wave moves between saw and square. Cutoff controls brightness by smoothing the wave's sharp edges: low is dark and soft, high is bright. The picture shows the shape you are hearing.
say.eli5: Turn the knobs while your tune plays. Wave changes the drawing from buzzy saw to video game square. Cutoff makes it darker or brighter, like turning a lamp down or up. Stop when you like it.

steps.q: What is sound?
steps.why: Something moves back and forth and pushes the air. Those pressure changes reach your ear as sound.

whyWrong.1: Electricity drives the speaker, but you hear the air the speaker moves.
whyWrong.2: Light is a different thing altogether. Sound travels through air.
whyWrong.3: The numbers describe the wave. It only becomes sound when a speaker moves the air.

steps.q: A synth has no string. So what actually moves the air?
steps.why: The synth makes the shape as numbers, and the speaker moves to that shape and pushes the air.

whyWrong.1: The numbers are the plan. The speaker is what physically moves.
whyWrong.2: Your screen just shows the picture.
whyWrong.3: You heard it, so something moved the air. That was the speaker.

steps.q: The high note had more wiggles packed into the picture. What does that mean?
options: the air moves back and forth faster
the wave is a different shape
steps.why: More cycles every second means faster vibration, and faster vibration is a higher pitch.

whyWrong.1: Loudness is how big the push is, not how often it happens.
whyWrong.2: Both notes were the same soft shape. Only the speed changed.
whyWrong.3: Both notes lasted the same time.

steps.q: Which wave sounds the smoothest and most pure?
steps.why: A round wave has no sharp corners, so there is nothing extra on top. It sounds pure.

whyWrong.1: The saw has a sudden drop, which makes it bright and buzzy.
whyWrong.2: The square jumps up and down suddenly, which gives it that hollow, game-like sound.
whyWrong.3: Same note, but the shapes sound clearly different. Go back and tap them again.

steps.q: Your synth sounds too harsh. Which knob helps most?
steps.why: Cutoff down smooths off the sharp edges of the wave, which is what makes it harsh.

whyWrong.1: Cutoff up keeps more of the sharp edges, so it gets even brighter.
whyWrong.2: The square is still full of sharp jumps.
whyWrong.3: Higher notes tend to sound even sharper.

steps.q: You mute the speaker but the wave still moves on screen. Can you hear it?
options: no, nothing is moving the air
yes, the synth is still playing
steps.why: Without a speaker moving, the numbers never become moving air, so there is no sound to hear.

whyWrong.1: The synth still makes the numbers, but no air moves.
whyWrong.2: No air moves at all, high or low.
whyWrong.3: The screen shows the picture, it does not move air.

steps.q: One full push and pull of the air is called what?
steps.why: One push and pull is a cycle. Pitch is how many cycles happen every second.

whyWrong.1: A beat is a step of the rhythm, like your kick.
whyWrong.2: A bar is four beats.
whyWrong.3: The shape is how each cycle looks, soft, saw or square.

steps.next: Next: louder and higher are not the same thing. You will hear the difference between volume and pitch.

lessons.title: hats

song.why: hats between the kicks lift the groove and make it move forward

lessons.learn: Open hats on the offbeat, the sound that makes house bounce, then closed hats on the sixteenths. Snap helps you place them.
youCan: play open hats on the offbeat with snap on
hear the lift an offbeat hat gives a groove
shape your hats with decay and tune

say.mentor: Kick on the beat, open hat exactly halfway between. Hear how it lifts? The kick pushes down, the hat pulls up, and the groove starts to bounce forward. This one pattern is the sound of a huge amount of house music.
say.straight: Open hats on the offbeat, halfway between the kicks. The kick goes down, the hat goes up, and the groove bounces.
say.eli5: Boom, tss, boom, tss. The tss goes right in between the booms. Hear how it makes the beat bounce?

say.mentor: Add hats to your song. Snap is on, set to eighths, so every hit lands exactly on the grid. Press rec, wait out the count-in, and tap the open hat between each kick: on every "and". Want a busier feel? Tap the snap key to change it to sixteenths and add some closed hats too.
say.straight: Record hats with snap on (eighths). Tap the open hat on every "and". Switch snap to sixteenths for closed hats if you want more.
say.eli5: Press rec, wait for four ticks, then tap the open hat in between every boom. The snap helper makes every tap land perfectly.

steps.hint: Count "one and two and" and tap on every "and".

say.mentor: Now shape them in your loop. Decay sets how long each hat rings: short and tight, or long and splashy. Tune moves them brighter or darker. A long, bright open hat feels big and open. A short, dark one sits back and lets the kick lead.
say.straight: Decay: how long each hat rings. Tune: brighter or darker. Shape them in your loop.
say.eli5: Decay makes the tss short or long. Tune makes it brighter or darker. Find the one you like.

steps.q: Where does the classic house open hat land?
options: on the offbeat, halfway between the kicks
steps.why: Halfway between the kicks, on every "and".

whyWrong.1: On the kick it would just thicken the kick.
whyWrong.2: Once a bar is too sparse for this sound.
whyWrong.3: Two and four is where the clap goes.

steps.q: What does snap do while you record?
options: moves each hit to the nearest grid line
steps.why: Snap pulls every hit onto the grid it's set to.

whyWrong.1: It moves notes, never deletes them.
whyWrong.2: It's about timing only.
whyWrong.3: The tempo stays the same.

steps.q: You want hats that sit back behind the kick. What do you try?
steps.why: Short and dark hats are less in your face.

whyWrong.1: That makes them bigger and more forward.
whyWrong.2: More hats is busier, not further back.
whyWrong.3: Tempo changes everything, not just the hats.

steps.next: Next: clap and snare. The backbeat on two and four, and the difference between the two.

lessons.title: clap and snare

song.why: a backbeat on two and four is what makes a beat feel like a groove

lessons.learn: The backbeat, the difference between a clap and a snare, and a snare in your song on two and four.
youCan: hear a clap from a snare
play a snare on two and four
say why house leans on claps and hip hop on snares

say.mentor: Kick on every beat, clap on two and four. That clap is the backbeat. Now listen closely to the clap itself: it's a few quick bursts of noise smeared together, like a handful of people clapping at once. A snare is different: a drum skin with metal wires underneath that rattle, so it has a body, a tone, and a sizzle on top.
say.straight: The clap on two and four is the backbeat. A clap is a few bursts of noise; a snare is a drum with rattling wires, so it has tone as well as noise.
say.eli5: Boom, clap, boom, clap. A clap is like hands clapping. A snare is a drum with tiny wires that buzz. Both go on two and four.

say.mentor: Put a snare in your song. Your kick keeps playing underneath. Press rec, wait out the count-in, and tap the snare on two and four. If your song already has a clap, they'll layer: a clap and snare together is a classic, fat backbeat.
say.straight: Record a snare on two and four over your kick. With a clap already there, they layer into a fatter backbeat.
say.eli5: Press rec, wait for four ticks, then tap the snare on two and on four.

steps.hint: Skip one, hit on two, skip three, hit on four.

say.mentor: House and techno lean on claps, a habit from the drum machines they grew up on, especially the Roland 909. Hip hop, rock and drum and bass lean on snares, often sampled from real kits. Lots of producers layer both and tune them until they sound like one hit.
say.straight: House and techno: mostly claps (the 909 sound). Hip hop and rock: mostly snares. Layering both is common.
say.eli5: Dance music likes claps. Hip hop and rock like snares. Lots of people use both at once.

deeper.title: the 909
deeper.say: Roland's TR-909 drum machine from 1983 has a clap and hats that shaped house and techno. Its clap is several noise bursts with a tail, almost exactly what's under your pad here.

steps.q: Where does the backbeat land?
steps.why: Two and four, answering the kick.

whyWrong.1: One and three are the kick on its own.
whyWrong.2: Every beat is the kick's job.
whyWrong.3: One is the start of the bar.

steps.q: What gives a snare its sizzle?
options: metal wires under the drum that rattle
steps.why: The snare wires rattle against the bottom skin.

whyWrong.1: Hands are a clap.
whyWrong.2: The rattle is the drum itself.
whyWrong.3: It's a separate drum.

steps.q: Which genre leans most on claps?
steps.why: House grew up on drum machine claps.

whyWrong.1: Rock leans on real snares.
whyWrong.2: Drum and bass is mostly sampled snares.
whyWrong.3: Jazz drummers use snares and brushes.

steps.next: Next: your first bass line, and why it has to share the low end with your kick.

lessons.title: your first bass line

song.why: the bass carries the weight and the harmony at the bottom of your track

lessons.learn: Bass notes on the keys, a bass line that grooves with your kick, and shaping it with cutoff and decay.
youCan: play a bass line into your song
place bass notes between the kicks so they groove
shape the bass with cutoff and decay

say.mentor: Low and high, the same note. Your bass lives down at the low end, where you feel it as much as hear it. In dance music the bass usually plays short notes between the kicks rather than on top of them, so the two take turns: kick, bass, kick, bass.
say.straight: The bass lives low. In dance music it often plays between the kicks so the two take turns.
say.eli5: Bass is the really low sound you feel in your tummy. It likes to go in between the booms, so the boom and the bass take turns.

say.mentor: Play a bass line into your song. Your kick plays along. Press rec, wait out the count-in, and play a few short notes in the gaps between kicks. Start on the first key, your song's home note, and try one or two others. Short and simple beats long and busy.
say.straight: Record a bass line in the gaps between kicks. Start on the first key, add one or two others, keep the notes short.
say.eli5: Press rec, wait for four ticks. Play short bass notes in between the booms. Start with the first key.

say.mentor: Shape it in your loop. Cutoff is the filter: low for a warm, round bass, higher for a buzzy one that cuts through on small speakers. Decay sets how long each note lasts: short and plucky, or long and rolling.
say.straight: Cutoff: warm and round when low, buzzy when high. Decay: plucky when short, rolling when long.
say.eli5: Cutoff makes the bass softer or buzzier. Decay makes each note short or long. Find a bass you like.

steps.q: Where does a dance music bass often sit?
steps.why: Between the kicks, so they take turns and don't pile up.

whyWrong.1: On top of the kick they fight for the same space.
whyWrong.2: Once a bar is very sparse.
whyWrong.3: Bass lives low.

steps.q: You want a bass that still cuts through on phone speakers. What do you try?
steps.why: Phone speakers can't play deep lows; brighter harmonics let the bass come through.

whyWrong.1: A very dark bass disappears on small speakers.
whyWrong.2: You'd barely hear it.
whyWrong.3: Tempo doesn't help.

steps.next: Next: make room. Your kick and bass both live down low, and you'll stop them fighting.

lessons.title: make room, kick and bass

song.why: a bass that ducks under the kick makes the low end punchy instead of muddy

lessons.learn: Why kick and bass fight, and the two classic fixes: shorter notes, and ducking the bass every time the kick hits.
youCan: hear when kick and bass are fighting
duck the bass under the kick
shorten the bass so it stays out of the kick's way

say.mentor: Your kick and your bass both live down low, below about 150 hz. When they hit at the same time they add up into a muddy, boomy blur, and the kick loses its punch. Every producer fights this, and there are two simple fixes you'll try on your own song.
say.straight: Kick and bass share the low end. When they overlap they turn to mud. Two fixes: shorter bass notes, and ducking.
say.eli5: The boom and the bass both live in the deep low part. When they happen together they get muddy, like two people talking at once.

say.mentor: Here's your song. Turn up duck: every time the kick hits, the bass dips out of the way for a moment and swells back. That's sidechain ducking, the pumping sound of so much dance music. Then try decay: shorter bass notes leave space for the kick too. Use a bit of both until the kick punches and the bass still rolls.
say.straight: Duck: the bass dips every time the kick hits (sidechain). Decay: shorter notes leave the kick room. Use both until the kick punches through.
say.eli5: Turn up duck: the bass gets quieter every time the boom hits, so they take turns. Then turn decay down to make bass notes shorter. Keep turning until both sound clear.

steps.q: Why do kick and bass fight?
options: they both live in the low end
the bass is always too quiet
the kick is out of tune
steps.why: Both sit below about 150 hz, so they pile up there.

whyWrong.1: Different sounds, same range.
whyWrong.2: Even at the right level they overlap.
whyWrong.3: Tuning doesn't cause the overlap.

steps.q: What does ducking the bass do?
options: dips the bass every time the kick hits
steps.why: The bass gets out of the kick's way and swells back.

whyWrong.1: The bass is still there between kicks.
whyWrong.2: It's quieter, briefly.
whyWrong.3: The notes stay the same.

steps.q: Ducking driven by another sound is called?
steps.why: Sidechain. The kick controls how much the bass dips.

whyWrong.1: Reverb is space.
whyWrong.2: Swing is timing.
whyWrong.3: Quantise is snap.

steps.next: Next: shape your synth properly. Resonance, envelopes, and a lead that moves.

lessons.title: shape your synth properly

song.why: the same notes can be a soft pad, a pluck or a squelchy lead, depending on how the sound moves

lessons.learn: Four controls every synth has: resonance, the filter envelope, attack and release, and your lead shaped with them.
youCan: say what resonance does to a filter
make a note brighten and close with the filter envelope
turn a lead into a pluck or a pad with attack and release

say.mentor: You've already used cutoff to make your lead darker or brighter. Now you'll make the sound move. Real synth sounds change during each note: they open up, sparkle, fade. Four knobs do most of it.
say.straight: Synth sounds move within each note. Four knobs control that: resonance, envelope, attack, release.
say.eli5: Good synth sounds change while the note plays. They open up and fade away. You'll learn four knobs that do it.

say.mentor:
Your lead, four knobs. Resonance makes the filter ring right at the cutoff, a whistly, squelchy peak. Envelope makes the filter open on every note and close again, so each note sparkles then darkens. Attack is how slowly a note fades in: zero for a pluck, high for a swell. Release is how long it rings after you let go.
Try a short attack, short release and lots of envelope for a pluck. Then long attack and long release for a pad.
say.straight: Res: a ringing peak at the cutoff. Env: the filter opens and closes on each note. Attack: fade in. Release: ring out. Pluck: short attack and release, lots of env. Pad: long attack and release.
say.eli5: Res makes it whistly. Env makes each note go bright then dark. Attack makes notes fade in slowly. Release makes them ring out after. Try a short pluck, then a long dreamy pad.

steps.q: What does resonance do?
options: adds a ringing peak at the cutoff
steps.why: Resonance boosts the frequencies right at the cutoff, a ringing peak.

whyWrong.1: That's release.
whyWrong.2: Synth knobs don't touch tempo.
whyWrong.3: Reverb is space, a different effect.

steps.q: For a pluck, what attack do you want?
steps.why: A pluck starts instantly.

whyWrong.1: Long attack is a swell, a pad.
whyWrong.2: Attack is most of what makes a pluck.
whyWrong.3: Release is a separate choice.

steps.q: What does the filter envelope do on each note?
options: opens the filter and lets it close again
steps.why: The filter opens then closes, so each note sparkles then darkens.

whyWrong.1: Pitch stays the same.
whyWrong.2: That's a delay or repeat.
whyWrong.3: Panning is left and right.

steps.next: Next: chords on top, pads or stabs, and the harmony that fills out your track.

lessons.title: chords on top

song.why: chords fill the middle of your track and set its mood

lessons.learn: Pads and stabs, the two ways chords sit in dance music, and chords in your song shaped either way.
youCan: play chords into your song
turn chords into long pads or short stabs
spread a chord wider

say.mentor: Chords in dance music usually do one of two jobs. Pads: long, soft chords that hold under everything, like a warm room. Stabs: short, punchy chords on the offbeat, like the piano hits in classic house. Same notes, completely different role.
say.straight: Chords are either pads (long, soft, underneath) or stabs (short, punchy, rhythmic).
say.eli5: Chords can be long and dreamy, called pads. Or short and punchy, called stabs. Same notes, different feel.

say.mentor: Play chords into your song. For pads, play two long chords, one per half bar. For stabs, tap short chords on the offbeats, between the kicks. Start on i, the home chord.
say.straight: Record chords: long ones for pads, short offbeat taps for stabs. Start on i.
say.eli5: Press rec. Hold two chords for pads, or tap short ones between the booms for stabs.

say.mentor: Release sets how long the chords ring: turn it up for a pad, down for a stab. Spread fans the notes of each chord wider apart, so it sounds bigger and more open.
say.straight: Release: long for pads, short for stabs. Spread: wider, bigger chords.
say.eli5: Release makes chords ring long or stop short. Spread makes them sound bigger.

steps.q: What's a stab?
steps.why: Short and punchy, often on the offbeat.

whyWrong.1: That's a pad.
whyWrong.2: Stabs are chords.
whyWrong.3: Reverb is space.

steps.q: To turn your chords into a pad, which knob do you turn up?
steps.why: Longer release lets each chord ring on.

whyWrong.1: Tempo is the whole song's speed.
whyWrong.2: That's the kick.
whyWrong.3: Swing is timing.

steps.next: Next: the kick designer. Build the best kick you can, from click to body.

lessons.title: the kick designer

song.why: the kick is the loudest thing in your track, so it's worth making it exactly right

lessons.learn: Every part of a kick you can shape: pitch, length, drive and level, and the best kick you can make for your song.
youCan: shape a kick's tune, decay, drive and level by ear
say what drive does to a kick
match a kick to the style of your track

say.mentor: You met decay and tune in your first lesson. Now you get the whole kick: four knobs, the ones producers reach for every time. Tap short and long again to remind your ears how much the length changes.
say.straight: Four kick controls: tune, decay, drive, level. You know two already.
say.eli5: Remember short and long kicks? Now you get four knobs to build your perfect kick.

say.mentor:
Your song, your kick. Tune sets how low the body sits: match it roughly to your bass so they don't clash. Decay sets how long it booms. Drive pushes the kick into soft distortion: it adds grit and harmonics, so it cuts through on small speakers. Level is how loud it sits against everything else.
Techno kicks tend to be driven and a bit longer. Deep house kicks are rounder and softer. Shape yours until it feels like your track.
say.straight: Tune: pitch of the body, near your bass. Decay: length. Drive: grit and presence. Level: loudness. Driven and long for techno, round and soft for deep house.
say.eli5: Tune makes the boom deeper or higher. Decay makes it short or long. Drive makes it crunchy. Level makes it louder or quieter. Play until it's your favourite kick.

steps.q: What does drive do to a kick?
options: adds grit and harmonics so it cuts through
steps.why: Soft distortion adds harmonics, which help it come through on small speakers.

whyWrong.1: Length is decay.
whyWrong.2: Kicks don't change the tempo.
whyWrong.3: Drive adds bite, it doesn't take the click away.

steps.q: Why tune the kick near the bass?
options: so the two low sounds don't clash
steps.why: Kick and bass share the low end; tuning them to fit avoids a muddy clash.

whyWrong.1: Level sets loudness.
whyWrong.2: Tuning doesn't touch tempo.
whyWrong.3: The bass plays its own notes.

steps.next: Next: drums from recordings. Swap your synth kit for a real one and hear the difference.

lessons.title: drums from recordings

song.why: recorded drums bring the texture of a real room and real hits into your track

lessons.learn: Synthesised drums against recorded ones, what a sampler does, and the kit your song uses.
youCan: say the difference between synth and sampled drums
say what a sampler does
choose a kit for your song by ear

say.mentor: Every drum you've used so far is made by the engine out of numbers: a sine for the kick's body, noise for the hats. Drum machines like the 909 did the same. The other way is to record real hits and play them back. That's what a sampler does: it plays a recording, at any pitch, whenever you hit a pad.
say.straight: Synth drums are generated. Sampled drums are recordings played back. A sampler plays a recording on every hit.
say.eli5: Your drums so far are made by the computer. Another way is to record real drums and play the recordings. A sampler does that.

say.mentor: Here's your own drum pattern on both kits. Switch between synth and recorded and listen to the texture: the recorded hits carry a bit of room and grit, the synth ones are cleaner and easier to shape. Lots of producers layer both. Pick the one that suits your song.
say.straight: Your pattern on the synth kit and the recorded kit. Recorded has more texture, synth is cleaner. Pick one.
say.eli5: Same beat, two drum kits. Tap synth, then recorded. Which do you like?

steps.q: What does a sampler do?
options: plays back a recording when you hit a pad
makes sound from a sine wave
steps.why: It plays a recorded sound, at any pitch, on every hit.

whyWrong.1: That's a synth.
whyWrong.2: Reverb is an effect.
whyWrong.3: It can play any recording.

steps.q: Why might a producer layer synth and recorded drums?
options: to get control and texture at once
steps.why: Synth gives shape and punch you can tweak; the recording adds texture.

whyWrong.1: Tempo is unchanged.
whyWrong.2: Samplers can play any drum.
whyWrong.3: Layering uses more, not less.

steps.next: Next: width and movement. Make your lead wide and alive.

lessons.title: width and movement

song.why: a lead that's wide and moves feels expensive; a static one feels flat

lessons.learn: Detune for width and glide for movement, on your own lead.
youCan: widen a sound with detune
add glide between notes
hear when a sound is too wide

say.mentor: Big synth leads are rarely one oscillator. Two or more play the same note, pulled very slightly out of tune with each other. They drift in and out, and your ears hear a thick, wide, moving sound. That's detune. Glide is the other trick: notes slide into each other instead of jumping.
say.straight: Detune: two oscillators slightly apart for a wide, thick sound. Glide: notes slide into each other.
say.eli5: Make two copies of a sound and put one a tiny bit out of tune: it sounds huge. That's detune. Glide makes notes slide like a trombone.

say.mentor: Your lead. Turn detune up slowly: first it thickens, then it shimmers, and too far it sounds out of tune and seasick. Find the edge and back off a bit. Then add some glide and listen to your melody slide between notes. A little goes a long way.
say.straight: Detune up until it thickens; back off before it sounds out of tune. Add a little glide.
say.eli5: Turn detune up until it sounds big but not wobbly. Then turn glide up a little and hear the notes slide.

steps.q: What does detune do?
options: makes a sound thicker and wider
steps.why: Slightly mistuned copies beat against each other and sound wide.

whyWrong.1: The notes stay in key; they're only a few cents apart.
whyWrong.2: Tempo stays the same.
whyWrong.3: Level is separate.

steps.q: What does glide do?
steps.why: Each note slides up or down into the next.

whyWrong.1: That's an arpeggiator or echo.
whyWrong.2: Reverb is space.
whyWrong.3: That's an eq.

steps.next: Next: risers. The noise sweep that tells the room a drop is coming.

lessons.title: fx, risers and sweeps

song.why: a riser builds tension so the drop lands harder

lessons.learn: What a riser is, why it works, and risers placed in your arrangement before the drops.
youCan: say what a riser does
place a riser before a drop
hear tension build and release

say.mentor: Before a big drop you'll almost always hear a sweep: noise or a synth rising in pitch and brightness over a few bars. That's a riser. It tells the whole room something is coming, and when it cuts off, the drop feels huge.
say.straight: A riser is a sweep up in pitch and brightness before a drop. It builds tension; the drop releases it.
say.eli5: Whoooosh, getting higher and higher, then BOOM. That whoosh is a riser. It makes everyone ready for the drop.

say.mentor: Here's your song laid out in sections. There's a riser row at the bottom. Tap it on for the section right before a drop and listen to the build. One per drop is plenty.
say.straight: Your arrangement. Turn a riser on in the section before a drop.
say.eli5: Find the part just before a drop and tap its riser. Then listen!

steps.q: Where does a riser usually go?
options: in the bars just before a drop
on beat one of the drop
in the middle of the intro
at the very end of the song
steps.why: It builds over the last bars before the drop and cuts off as it lands.

whyWrong.1: On the drop it would get in the way.
whyWrong.2: It needs something to build towards.
whyWrong.3: There's nothing to build to there.

steps.next: Next: levels and balance. The mix starts here.

lessons.title: levels and balance

song.why: a mix is mostly getting the levels right, and the lead is where most people get it wrong

lessons.learn: Balancing your parts by ear: where the lead sits against the beat, and placing it left or right.
youCan: set a part's level by ear against the rest of the song
pan a part left or right
say why mixing starts with levels

say.mentor: Most of mixing is just levels: how loud each part is against the others. Get those right and a track already sounds nearly finished. Producers usually start with the kick, set everything else around it, and come back to the lead last, because it's the easiest one to set too loud.
say.straight: Mixing starts with levels. Set the kick first, build around it, and check the lead last; it's usually too loud.
say.eli5: Mixing means making every sound the right loudness so they all fit. Start with the boom, then the rest.

say.mentor: Here's your song with level and pan on your lead. Pull the level down until you can only just hear the melody, then bring it up slowly and stop the moment it feels clear. That's usually lower than you'd guess. Then try pan: a little left or right gives it its own place on the stage, away from the kick and bass in the middle.
say.straight: Lead level: pull it down until barely audible, then up until clear, and stop. Pan: a little off centre frees the middle for kick and bass.
say.eli5: Turn level down until you can barely hear your tune, then turn it up slowly until it's just clear. Pan moves it left or right.

steps.q: Where do most producers start a mix?
options: the kick, then build around it
the lead, as loud as possible
steps.why: The kick is the anchor; everything else is set against it.

whyWrong.1: Leads set first tend to end up too loud.
whyWrong.2: Reverb comes once levels are set.
whyWrong.3: Hats are set against the kick too.

steps.q: Why keep the kick and bass in the middle?
options: they carry the low end, which should hit both speakers equally
steps.why: Low end in the middle stays solid on any speaker system.

whyWrong.1: They're usually the loudest.
whyWrong.2: Panning works on anything.
whyWrong.3: Panning has nothing to do with speed.

steps.next: Next: eq. Give every part its own slice of the frequencies.

lessons.title: eq, a place for everything

song.why: cutting the lows out of your lead leaves the low end clean for the kick and bass

lessons.learn: What an eq does, the low cut that cleans up almost every mix, and shaping your lead's tone.
youCan: say what an eq does
use a low cut to clear the low end
boost or cut lows, mids and highs by ear

say.mentor: An eq, short for equaliser, turns parts of the sound up or down by frequency: lows, mids, highs. It's how you give every part its own place. Your lead doesn't need the deep lows, so cutting them leaves that space for the kick and bass. Almost every part in a mix gets a low cut except those two.
say.straight: An eq boosts or cuts lows, mids and highs. A low cut on everything except kick and bass keeps the low end clean.
say.eli5: An eq is like a set of tone knobs for low, middle and high sounds. You take away the low rumble from your tune so the boom and bass have room.

say.mentor: Your lead, four eq knobs. Low cut removes everything below the frequency you set: turn it up until the lead starts to sound thin, then back off a touch. Low, mid and high boost or cut those bands. Try a small mid cut if the lead sounds boxy, a little high boost if it needs air.
say.straight: Low cut: up until thin, then back a touch. Low, mid, high: boost or cut. Mid cut for boxiness, high boost for air.
say.eli5: Turn low cut up until your tune sounds thin, then back a little. Then play with low, mid and high.

steps.q: Which parts usually keep their lows?
steps.why: Kick and bass own the low end. Most other parts get a low cut.

whyWrong.1: The lead usually gets a low cut.
whyWrong.2: Hats are all highs.
whyWrong.3: Reverb lows get muddy fast.

steps.q: A sound is boxy. What might you try?
options: a small cut in the mids
a big boost in the lows
steps.why: Boxiness usually lives in the mids.

whyWrong.1: That adds mud.
whyWrong.2: Reverb would smear it.
whyWrong.3: Tempo won't change tone.

steps.next: Next: space. Reverb and echo, and how near or far each part sounds.

lessons.title: space, reverb and echo

song.why: a little reverb and echo puts your lead in a room instead of right in your ear

lessons.learn: Reverb and echo, sends, and how much space to give your lead.
youCan: say the difference between reverb and echo
send your lead to reverb and echo
hear near and far in a mix

say.mentor: Reverb is the sound of a room: thousands of tiny reflections blurring into a tail. Echo, or delay, is a clear repeat of the sound. Dry sounds feel close, right in your ear. More reverb pushes them further back. Producers use that to give a mix depth: kick and bass up front and dry, pads and leads a little further back.
say.straight: Reverb: a room's blur of reflections. Echo: clear repeats. More of either pushes a sound further back.
say.eli5: Reverb makes a sound feel like it's in a big room. Echo makes it repeat, echo, echo. More of either makes it feel further away.

say.mentor: Your lead with two sends. Send goes to the reverb, echo to the echo. A send means a copy of your lead goes to the effect while the dry lead stays as it is, so you blend in just as much space as you want. Start low. A little is usually plenty.
say.straight: Send: how much lead goes to reverb. Echo: how much to the echo. The dry sound stays; you blend in space. Start low.
say.eli5: Send adds a big-room sound. Echo adds repeats. A little bit is usually enough.

steps.q: What's the difference between reverb and echo?
options: reverb is a blur of reflections, echo is clear repeats
steps.why: Reverb smears, echo repeats.

whyWrong.1: They sound very different.
whyWrong.2: Loudness isn't the difference.
whyWrong.3: Reverb works on anything.

steps.q: More reverb on a part makes it sound?
steps.why: Wet sounds sit back; dry sounds sit up front.

whyWrong.1: Dry is close.
whyWrong.2: Tempo is unchanged.
whyWrong.3: Pitch is unchanged.

steps.next: Next: glue. The mix as one sound, loud and clean.

lessons.title: glue, compression and loudness

song.why: a little bus compression makes your parts sound like one record instead of separate sounds

lessons.learn: The glue compressor on the master, the limiter after it, and how loud is loud enough.
youCan: say what a bus compressor does
add glue to your mix by ear
say what a limiter is for

say.mentor: Mastering engineers talk about glue: when every part of a track breathes together like one record. Most of that comes from a gentle compressor across the whole mix. It turns the loudest moments down a touch, so everything moves as one. After it, a limiter catches any peaks so the song never clips.
say.straight: Glue is a compressor across the whole mix: it pulls the parts together. A limiter after it stops clipping.
say.eli5: Glue makes all your sounds feel like one band playing together. A limiter stops it ever getting too loud and crackly.

say.mentor: Your whole song. Turn glue up and listen to how the drums and bass start to pump and lock together. Too much and it sounds squashed and tired. Out sets how hard the mix hits the limiter: louder, but push it too far and the punch goes. Find the point where it sounds like a finished record.
say.straight: Glue up until the mix locks together, before it sounds squashed. Out sets loudness into the limiter; too much loses punch.
say.eli5: Turn glue up until everything feels tight. Then turn out up until it's nice and loud, but not crunchy.

steps.q: What does a glue compressor on the master do?
options: pulls the parts together so they move as one
steps.why: Gentle compression across the mix makes it breathe together.

whyWrong.1: That's a delay.
whyWrong.2: Compression doesn't touch tempo.
whyWrong.3: It treats everything.

steps.q: What is a limiter for?
steps.why: It catches peaks so nothing goes over the top.

whyWrong.1: Width is detune, pan or stereo effects.
whyWrong.2: Tuning is on the kick.
whyWrong.3: Swing is timing.

steps.next: Next: sections. Your loop becomes a song.

lessons.title: sections

song.why: a loop becomes a song when parts come and go

lessons.learn: Intro, build, drop and break, and your loop turned into a full arrangement by switching parts on and off.
youCan: name the sections of a dance track
arrange your parts across sections
hear how removing a part makes its return bigger

say.mentor: A dance track is mostly the same loop, changed by taking things away and bringing them back. An intro for djs to mix in, a build, the drop where everything plays, a break where the drums disappear, and the drop again. Nothing new is written. It's all arrangement.
say.straight: Intro, build, drop, break, drop. Mostly the same loop with parts switched in and out.
say.eli5: A song is your loop with bits turned on and off. Start small, build up, everything at once, take the drums away, then bring it all back.

say.mentor: Here's your song as five sections, already laid out the classic way. Each row is one of your parts, each column a section. Tap a cell to switch that part off or on there. Play it through and change it until the journey feels right.
say.straight: Rows are parts, columns sections. Tap cells to switch parts off or on. Play it and adjust.
say.eli5: Tap the squares to turn sounds on or off in each part of your song. Press play and listen.

steps.q: Why do intros often start without the bass?
options: so djs can mix the track in cleanly
steps.why: A sparse intro leaves room to blend from the previous track.

whyWrong.1: It's a choice, not a limit.
whyWrong.2: Tempo stays the same.
whyWrong.3: Intros usually do have drums.

steps.q: Where does everything usually play at once?
steps.why: The drop is the peak.

whyWrong.1: The intro is sparse.
whyWrong.2: The break takes things away.
whyWrong.3: The outro thins out for the next track.

steps.next: Next: fills. One bar that's different, right before things change.

lessons.title: variation and fills

song.why: a fill signals that something is about to change

lessons.learn: What a fill is, where it goes, and fills at the ends of your sections.
youCan: say what a fill does
place fills at section ends
hear how a fill sets up a change

say.mentor: A drummer playing the same beat for four minutes still tells you when something's coming: a roll on the snare at the end of a section. That's a fill. In dance music it might be a snare roll, the kick dropping out for a beat, or a burst of hats. Whatever it is, it says: change ahead.
say.straight: A fill is a short variation, often the last beat or bar of a section, that signals a change.
say.eli5: A fill is a little drum roll at the end of a part that says, get ready, something new is coming!

say.mentor: Your arrangement has a fill row. Tap fill on a section and its last beat drops the kick for a quick snare roll. Put fills before the drop and the break and listen to how they lead you in.
say.straight: Tap fill on sections that lead into a change. The last beat becomes a snare roll.
say.eli5: Tap fill on the part before the drop. Listen to the drum roll.

steps.q: What does a fill tell the listener?
steps.why: It's a signal that the next section is about to start.

whyWrong.1: It leads into something.
whyWrong.2: Tempo stays the same.
whyWrong.3: It's one of the clearest signals in music.

steps.next: Next: the breakdown and the drop, the biggest moment in your track.

lessons.title: the breakdown and the drop

song.why: taking the drums away makes their return the biggest moment in the track

lessons.learn: Why a breakdown makes a drop hit, and the drop in your own arrangement.
youCan: build a breakdown by removing the drums
bring everything back for a drop
hear tension and release

say.mentor: The moment a room screams is almost never a new sound. It's an old one coming back. Take the kick out for 8 or 16 bars, let the melody and pads float, build with a riser, then slam the kick back in. The absence is what makes the return feel huge.
say.straight: Breakdown: drums out. Drop: drums back. The gap is what makes the drop hit.
say.eli5: Take the boom away for a while. Everyone waits. Then BOOM, it comes back, and everyone jumps.

say.mentor: Take the drums out of one section and bring them back in the next. Add a riser and a fill before the drop if you like. Play it through and feel it land.
say.straight: Switch drums off in one section and on in the next. Riser and fill optional.
say.eli5: Turn off the drums in one part, then turn them back on in the next part. Press play and wait for the drop.

steps.q: Why does a drop feel big?
options: the drums were missing just before
steps.why: Contrast. After the break, the drums return with full force.

whyWrong.1: It's usually the same level; it just feels bigger.
whyWrong.2: The tempo stays.
whyWrong.3: It's the same song.

steps.next: Next: finish and export. Name it, take it to Live, send it to CCD.

lessons.title: finish and export

song.why: a song is finished when it leaves the app

lessons.learn: Naming your song, exporting it as midi for Ableton Live, and what happens next.
youCan: export your song as midi
open it in Live and keep working
say what stems are

say.mentor:
Lots of producers have hundreds of loops and no finished songs. Finishing is a skill, and you've just done it: a beat, a bass, a lead, chords, a mix and an arrangement, all yours.
From here you can take it into Ableton Live to keep going: more sounds, vocals, a proper master. You export it as midi, the notes of every part, and Live plays them on its own instruments.
say.straight: Finishing matters. Export your song as midi and open it in Live to keep going.
say.eli5: You made a whole song! Now you can take it into a big music program called Ableton Live.

deeper.title: stems
deeper.say: Stems are each part exported as its own audio file: drums, bass, lead and so on. Engineers and djs use them to remix and master. They're coming to CCD School soon.

say.mentor: Here's your finished song. Give it a name, play it through once more, and download the midi. Drop the file into Live and every part lands on its own track. And if you're proud of it, send it to CCD: the best learner tracks get played at our nights.
say.straight: Name it, play it, download the midi, open it in Live. Send it to CCD if you're proud of it.
say.eli5: Type a name for your song. Then tap download and open it in Live.

steps.q: What does a midi file hold?
steps.why: Midi is notes, timing and velocity. Live plays them on its instruments.

whyWrong.1: That's an audio export.
whyWrong.2: It holds every part.
whyWrong.3: It's music data only.
